transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-11-05 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martens (Redwood SE), Nina Rao (Palisade - Head of Cloud Security), Marcus Lee (Palisade - Platform Eng), Sofia Patel (Palisade - Compliance)

[00:00] Laura Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh before we get into the deep arch we just wanted a quick run through of goals, nina could you, you know, remind us the primary constraints?
[00:12] Nina Rao: yep, main constraints are regulatory data residency, we need all inference to occur inside our VPC in us-east-1, no egress other than to our approved S3 buckets and internal SIEM, also SOC 2 controls around auditability, ok?
[00:27] Marcus Lee: and from infra side we have transit gateway to a partner network, so we need clear guidance for peering vs vpc endpoints, and we prefer no public internet egress from the inference hosts.
[00:40] Diego Martens: great, so what we'll show is the typical Redwood Private pattern: private control plane, customer-managed data plane in your VPC, and options for either VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, or VPC endpoints depending on your topology.
[00:55] Sofia Patel: quick Q — are audit logs sent to our SIEM or Redwood stores them? we need retention and tamper-evidence details.
[01:03] Laura Chen: good question — by default audit logs are pushed to your logging endpoint; Redwood stores minimal control-plane metadata for support with customer-controlled retention. Diego will go into the KMS and logging flows.
[01:14] Diego Martens: right, on KMS we integrate with your CMKs. For on-prem or air-gapped we support HSM-backed keys; for cloud we perform envelope encryption with your KMS — Redwood doesn't hold plaintext model checkpoints or customer payloads.
[01:29] Marcus Lee: so keys live in our account, and Redwood has no ability to decrypt?
[01:33] Diego Martens: correct — customer-managed keys, we only get a short-lived grant scoped to the instance and it is revokable. There is some nuance with shared kernels but we can walk through policies.
[01:44] Nina Rao: about network — we want to ensure no unexpected egress, how are software updates handled for the runtime if instances cannot reach internet?
[01:52] Laura Chen: two options, you can allow a restricted egress to Redwood update mirrors via a proxy, or we can ship curated AMIs/containers that you control and update via your internal image pipeline.
[02:05] Marcus Lee: would prefer image-based patching, less outbound rules to manage.
[02:09] Diego Martens: noted. For ingress, we recommend a private internal ALB or NLB with TLS mutual auth; clients connect to private endpoints in your subnets, and we run the inference pods in customer subnets behind strict SGs.
[02:25] [Diego shares architecture link in chat: https://redwood.example.com/arch/palisade-private-vpc]
[02:30] Sofia Patel: we also need RBAC and SSO — can we map our roles from SAML to Redwood roles, and SCIM provisioning?
[02:38] Laura Chen: yes, SAML for SSO and SCIM for provisioning is supported — you can map LDAP groups to Redwood roles and have RBAC enforced at the API and console level.
[02:47] Nina Rao: about audit logs — retention policy for logs forwarded to our SIEM, but what about write-once logs in Redwood for supportable forensics?
[02:57] Diego Martens: we support forwarding syslog/CloudWatch events to your SIEM. Additionally, for tamper-evidence we ship hash chains for critical audit events into a customer-owned storage. It's not blockchain, it's HMAC chains, but it's for the same purpose.
[03:14] Marcus Lee: ok, can you show sample firewall rules for egress? we need explicit allow list.
[03:20] Diego Martens: sure, typical pattern: deny all egress by default; allow 1) your SIEM IP ranges on 443 to our logging endpoint, 2) S3 endpoints for model artifacts via VPC endpoint, 3) KMS endpoint to your KMS endpoint, 4) optionally Redwood update mirror IPs. We will share a Terraform snippet.
[03:39] [03:39] Laura Chen: I'll attach the TF snippet after the call.
[03:43] Nina Rao: about bastion access — we require session recording for any interactive access to the nodes, can Redwood integrate with our bastion and SSM?
[03:51] Diego Martens: yes, we can integrate with SSM Session Manager for exec access, or you can route via your bastion and we disable SSH on instances. Session logs can be forwarded to your logging pipeline.
[04:02] Marcus Lee: what about intra-zone encryption for KV cache? we have PCI segments so any KV cache storing sensitive context must be encrypted in transit and at rest.
[04:11] Diego Martens: KV cache traffic is mTLS, and at rest it's encrypted with your CMK. For higher isolation we can pin cache replicas to private subnets with customer-controlled security groups.
[04:22] Sofia Patel: can we get SOC 2 and ISO27001 certs and the control mappings? we need to present to auditors.
[04:29] Laura Chen: yes, SOC 2 attestation and ISO documents are in our security pack, I'll send those. They include mappings and our shared responsibility matrix.
[04:36] Nina Rao: about egress inspection — we prefer egress through our proxy stack for DLP and IDS, is that supported?
[04:43] Diego Martens: absolutely, you can route egress through your proxy via NAT gateway or through a forward proxy with auth. We'll document how to configure the outbound host header and TLS passthrough.
[04:54] Marcus Lee: great. Now the tricky bit — model downloads and updates, we need to ensure model artifacts never go to public internet and are signed.
[05:02] Diego Martens: models are pulled from a private S3 bucket or your artifact registry. We support verifying signatures on artifacts and can require signed manifests and checksums.
[05:12] Nina Rao: retention for request/response logs — we have privacy regs, so we need redaction or minimal logging. Can Redwood redact PII at ingest?
[05:20] Laura Chen: we have configurable logging levels; you can opt-out of storing full request/response and instead store only hashed request ids and partial metadata. For PII redaction, we can run a filter pipeline before logs are emitted, that can be customer-managed.
[05:34] [05:34] Diego Martens: Also worth noting fallback patterns: if your capacity is insufficient we can failover to a dedicated-host model variant in your private deployment, but that's only with approved cross-account peering and strict controls.
[05:47] Marcus Lee: what's the network path for control plane telemetry? we don't want control plane to bypass our egress restrictions.
[05:54] Diego Martens: the control plane talks to the control plane endpoints in your account via PrivateLink or peering; we can configure the control plane to send minimal telemetry over your internal endpoints.
[06:05] Sofia Patel: compliance question — how do you support data residency across regions for multi-region failover?
[06:12] Laura Chen: you can pin workloads to a region and configure cross-region replication for artifacts only if you opt in. For failover we can spin up in a DR region but only with replicated artifacts under your control and with explicit approvals.
[06:25] [06:25] Nina Rao: Marcus — are there any constraints from our infra side?
[06:28] Marcus Lee: our main limit is that we cannot open inbound internet to the inference subnets, and all egress must hit our egress proxy. NAT is allowed but only to proxy.
[06:36] Diego Martens: perfect — in that case our recommended deploy is private NLB in your subnets + VPC endpoints for S3 + egress NAT to proxy. We'll provide the SG and NACL examples.
[06:48] [Diego shares: sample-sg.tf and egress-policy.yaml in chat]
[06:53] Sofia Patel: about key rotation — we need yearly rotation and immediate revocation on incident, can we revoke keys and cause sessions to expire?
[07:01] Diego Martens: yes, revoking grants in KMS will invalidate active sessions for any subsequent decryption ops; we can also force a rekey on the runtime and restart processes under your control. We'll document the exact window.
[07:12] Nina Rao: will Redwood maintain full packet captures for troubleshooting? we need to ensure those are not stored long-term.
[07:19] Laura Chen: we don't retain PCAPs; we recommend ephemeral captures pushed to your S3 for forensics controlled by your retention policies.
[07:28] Marcus Lee: ok good. Any third-party service calls? like license checks or telemetry to third parties?
[07:34] Diego Martens: no third-party outbound calls except optional telemetry endpoints you opt into; all third-party libs are vendored in the image.
[07:42] Sofia Patel: one more — do you support FIPS endpoints and hardened crypto stacks for the HSM?
[07:48] Diego Martens: yes, FIPS-compliant crypto modules are supported when using HSM-backed keys; we'll include the list of supported modules.
[07:57] [08:00] Laura Chen: wrap up — recap of agreed items and next steps. Diego, you'll send TF snippets and the architecture doc; I'll send SOC2/ISO pack and pricing for private deployment. Customer to share CIDRs and proxy details.
[08:12] Nina Rao: sounds good. Marcus and I will review and get back with any further constraints. Thanks.
[08:19] Laura Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts and schedule the pilot onboarding.
[08:23] [End of recording]

Notes on transcription: minor transcription errors in acronyms present; speaker labels are mostly accurate but a few lines may be merged due to simultaneous talk. Links shared in chat: https://redwood.example.com/arch/palisade-private-vpc , sample-sg.tf, egress-policy.yaml
notes: Architecture diagram and Terraform snippets shared in chat; action items captured above. Some acronym mis-transcriptions (e.g., KV cache spelled K-V cache or 'kay-vee') are present.
